messages.subject: [statnet_help] mapply() and dyadcov term
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have 31 networks with which I am working (playmate ties of children in
villages; no cross-village ties) in a list object (i.e., each network is an
object in the list). Because I have these 31 networks in a list and I'm
fitting the same model, I have been using lapply() for ease of coding and
efficiency. I've fit a variety of ERGMs on these networks with no problems.
I'm now trying to fit one with a dyadic covariates (matrices of geographic
distance from child-to-child in each of the village networks) using the
mapply() function with the list of 31 networks and a corresponding list of
31 matrices.

When I add in the "dyadcov" term to the ERGM and use the mapply() function,
I get the following error: *Error in check.ErgmTerm(nw, arglist, varnames =
c("x", "attrname"), vartypes = c("matrix,network",  : object 'y' not found*,
where 'y' is parameter name (in the mapply() function) for the matrix in
the "dyadcov" term.

However, if I specify the ERGM with a particular network from the list
object and a particular matrix from the list object, the ERGM estimation
works just fine. Does anyone have thoughts as to what's going on? I'm at a
loss as to why the mapply() approach doesn't work and the other does.

I've included reproducible code below and I'm using R 3.0.0 and statnet
3.1-0 (ergm 3.1-0) on a MacBook Pro.

Thanks for listening!

Matt

# libraries
library(statnet)

# create network object
set.seed(02122013)
net <- network(rgraph(55, tprob = .1))

# create symmetric matrix (representing distances (say, in kilometers)
between nodes)
set.seed(02122013)
dist.mtx <- matrix(rnorm(3025), nr = 55, nc = 55)
diag(dist.mtx) <- 0
dist.mtx <- symmetrize(dist.mtx, rule = "upper")
dist.mtx[dist.mtx < 0] <- 0

# create list objects
net <- list(net)
dist.mtx <- list(dist.mtx)

# specifying objects directly (no issues in estimating)
mod1 <- ergm(net[[1]] ~ edges + mutual + twopath + gwidegree(2) +
gwodegree(2) + gwesp(log(2)) + ctriple + dyadcov(dist.mtx[[1]]), control =
control.ergm(MCMLE.maxit = 8))
params <- enformulate.curved(mod1)
mod2 <- ergm(params$formula, control = control.ergm(init = params$theta,
MCMLE.maxit = 20, MCMC.burnin = 100000, MCMC.interval = 1000,
MCMC.samplesize = 15000))

# using mapply function (problem after the 'mod1' code)
model <- mapply(function(x, y) {
mod1 <- ergm(x ~ edges + mutual + twopath + gwidegree(2) +
gwodegree(2) + gwesp(log(2)) + ctriple + dyadcov(y), control =
control.ergm(MCMLE.maxit = 8))
params <- enformulate.curved(mod1)
mod2 <- ergm(params$formula, control = control.ergm(init = params$theta,
MCMLE.maxit = 20, MCMC.burnin = 100000, MCMC.interval = 1000,
MCMC.samplesize = 15000))
return(list(mod2))
}, net, dist.mtx)

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Statistical methods for a sample of networks
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Statistical methods for a sample of networks
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

*Warning: This email is a little long*

I am a social psychologist by training and am new to social network
analysis.  I am planning a series of studies that involve small groups of
people.  In a typical study, the participants will meet in groups of 4 to
have a discussion about a particular topic.  As a group, the participants
will reach a decision about the topic (e.g., whether to support or oppose a
proposed change in university policy).  The discussion will be videotaped,
and we will use transcripts of the discussion to obtain information about
who is talking to whom about what topics.  In addition, the participants
will complete ratings of themselves and each other (e.g., What is your
opinion about the proposed change?  What do you think is this person's
opinion of the proposed change?).  I will also have a variety of data about
the individual characteristics of all the participants.  Thus, each group
from each study will give me a 4-node network with directed, valued edges
and a variety of attributes about each node.

In all the studies, I will be interested in group-level,
relationship-level, and individual-level outcomes.  I have provided below a
sampling of the kinds of questions I would want to ask from these data:

(1) Which groups express the most agreement in their discussions?  Which
groups express the most disagreement?  Is group composition related to
agreement / disagreement and to the final decision outcome?
(2) Which pairs of people like each other during the discussion?  Which
pairs of people dislike each other?  How are the pairwise patterns of
liking related to the final decision outcome?
(3) Who has the most influence on the course of the discussion?  Who has
influence over the final decision of each group?  Are there any individual
difference characteristics that are related to influence over the
discussion and / or final decision?

And so on.  What I am looking for from the mailing list is the proper
statistical model to use to investigate *samples* of networks, rather than
individual networks.  I have read a bit about single-network methods, like
ERGM models, but these methods do not seem appropriate, since I am dealing
with a set of independent networks, rather than a single network.  In
addition, a plain linear mixed model does not seem appropriate because I am
collecting relational data.  Finally, although a method like the social
relations model seems appropriate for this situation at first blush, the
social relations model seems to only partition the variance in round-robin
ratings into perceiver, target, and relationship sources rather than
allowing me to, for example, relate the patterns within a set of networks
to overall network outcomes.

Perhaps I'm over-thinking this problem, and perhaps the choice of the
appropriate statistical model is obvious.  However, as I mentioned earlier
in the email, I am new to this stuff.  Could anyone offer some advice about
which statistical model might be appropriate for my situation?  Also, is
the proper analytic method possible in statnet?

-- 
Patrick S Forscher
PhD Candidate
University of Wisconsin-Madison

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Statistical methods for a sample of networks
messages.body_plain:
Hi Patrick,

If you can reasonably assume that the data-generating process is the 
same for all networks, you can combine them in a single matrix and use 
structural zeros for the between-network dyads which cannot have any 
connection. The problem is rather that there are not a lot of ways to 
model weighted network data. There are simply no model terms available 
for generalized ERGMs or count ERGMs (unless somebody from the statnet 
team has recently implemented some model terms for valued networks, 
which I don't know). See here: help("ergm-terms", package = 
"ergm.count"). If the timing of the edges matters, relational event 
models may be an alternative (look at the articles of Carter Butts and 
Brandes/Lerner/Snijders and at the relevent package). On the other hand, 
the questions you are asking are more related to explaining outcomes per 
network and describing the networks in terms of centrality. So I am not 
sure if you need a model which explains network formation at all. It may 
be more interesting for you to describe the network in terms of who is 
central (or any other interesting graph statistics) and use them as 
covariates when you model the outcomes of your networks (since they are 
independent by design).

As for the conversion of your transcripts into network matrices, this is 
not a trivial task. I wrote a Java software package for this purpose. 
It's called Discourse Network Analyzer (see www.github.com/leifeld/dna). 
Right now, however, you can only annotate what each person says (and 
whether the person agrees or disagrees with the concept). You can then 
produce two-mode network matrices of actors and concepts, or one-mode 
network matrices where two actors are connected if they have claims in 
common (both agreeing to the same concepts or both disagreeing to the 
same concepts). It is not possible right now to annotate direct 
connections between actors (at least not with additional qualifiers 
other than positive and negative). But I am working on a new version 
with more flexible ways of annotating text data and extracting networks 
from them.

Best,
Philip

Hi Philip, thanks very much for your reply!  From your description, it
sounds like, for any models that relate to group-level outcomes (e.g., the
decisions made by each group), it might be reasonable to extract the
relevant network statistics from each network and fit a regular logistic
regression -- is that correct?

However, some of the questions that I'm interested in relate to
individual-level outcomes.  For example, if I were interested in predicting
who has the most influence on the conversation (i.e., who is most central),
it seems to me that any statistical model that I fit to answer this
question should take into account the explicitly relational nature of the
study design.  In most of these cases, the outcome variable will be
measured on either an interval scale, and could either be a derived measure
(i.e., network centrality, in-degree / in-strength) or a raw measure (i.e.,
time spent speaking, participant self-ratings of how much they enjoyed the
discussion, etc).  In these cases, what options do I have given the design
of these studies?

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Statistical methods for a sample of networks
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Patrick.  Just to add to what folks have already said, you might 
also find the following paper useful:

Butts, Carter T.  2011.  Bayesian meta-analysis of social network data 
via conditional uniform graph quantiles.  Sociological Methodology, 
41(1): 257-298. 
http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1467-9531.2011.01240.x/abstract

The approach described in that paper can be used to e.g. test hypotheses 
regarding structural biases across treatments, among other things.

Note that, if your data and hypotheses are group-level, they can be 
tested without any particularly network-specific techniques; for 
instance, a standard permutation test (or, for that matter, any of a 
range of similar procedures) can be used to test hypotheses regarding 
the association between a treatment and a graph-level index (e.g., 
degree centralization).  Just because your data involve networks does 
not per se mean that you need to use special procedures.  (It all 
depends on the details of your analysis.)  For some examples, you might 
want to look at the materials from our "Beyond Descriptives" statnet 
workshop (archived at www.statnet.org).

As far as pooled analysis of ERGMs, you can see some of our 
work-in-progress on this front at Sunbelt in February!  It's certainly 
doable (although, with only four nodes in each network, you will have 
little power to distinguish among competing structural mechanisms) - but 
for at least some of your questions, it may not be the tool you need.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

> of 4 to have a discussion about a particular topic.  As a group, the 
> participants will reach a decision about the topic (e.g., whether to 
> support or oppose a proposed change in university policy).  The 
> discussion will be videotaped, and we will use transcripts of the 
> discussion to obtain information about who is talking to whom about 
> what topics.  In addition, the participants will complete ratings of 
> themselves and each other (e.g., What is your opinion about the 
> proposed change?  What do you think is this person's opinion of the 
> proposed change?).  I will also have a variety of data about the 
> individual characteristics of all the participants.  Thus, each group 
> from each study will give me a 4-node network with directed, valued 
> edges and a variety of attributes about each node.
>
> In all the studies, I will be interested in group-level, 
> relationship-level, and individual-level outcomes.  I have provided 
> below a sampling of the kinds of questions I would want to ask from 
> these data:
>
> (1) Which groups express the most agreement in their discussions? 
>  Which groups express the most disagreement?  Is group composition 
> related to agreement / disagreement and to the final decision outcome?
> (2) Which pairs of people like each other during the discussion? 
>  Which pairs of people dislike each other?  How are the pairwise 
> patterns of liking related to the final decision outcome?
> (3) Who has the most influence on the course of the discussion?  Who 
> has influence over the final decision of each group?  Are there any 
> individual difference characteristics that are related to influence 
> over the discussion and / or final decision?
>
> And so on.  What I am looking for from the mailing list is the proper 
> statistical model to use to investigate /samples/ of networks, rather 
> than individual networks.  I have read a bit about single-network 
> methods, like ERGM models, but these methods do not seem appropriate, 
> since I am dealing with a set of independent networks, rather than a 
> single network.  In addition, a plain linear mixed model does not seem 
> appropriate because I am collecting relational data.  Finally, 
> although a method like the social relations model seems appropriate 
> for this situation at first blush, the social relations model seems to 
> only partition the variance in round-robin ratings into perceiver, 
> target, and relationship sources rather than allowing me to, for 
> example, relate the patterns within a set of networks to overall 
> network outcomes.
>
> Perhaps I'm over-thinking this problem, and perhaps the choice of the 
> appropriate statistical model is obvious.  However, as I mentioned 
> earlier in the email, I am new to this stuff.  Could anyone offer some 
> advice about which statistical model might be appropriate for my 
> situation?  Also, is the proper analytic method possible in statnet?
>
> -- 
> Patrick S Forscher
